MX17 response simulation · T14 · 13 Oct 2026

The sim/data gap points to two known gas-physics effects the chain leaves out: avalanche photon feedback, and a drifting ion that is a hydrocarbon fragment, not Ar⁺

Evidence: 3 chambers × 3 gases from the April–June cosmic bench, plus SPS. Literature: both effects are described before, and the gain form used here is the field’s standard one.

1

Details

Two separate effects, each now constrained by more than one chamber and more than one gas, account for T14's oldest rows: the gain slope and amplitude, and the rise time / ion signal. Neither is a new idea. Both have a literature, summarised on slides 5 and 8.

Source of every number: MX17_Geant/design/report/FRESH_LOOK_2026-10-12.md §12–13; scripts and logs in MX17_Geant/scratchpad/2026-10-13c/.

2

Details

T14 compares the full chain (Geant4 → drift → Garfield avalanche → induction kernels → ion template → DREAM shaper) with det3 cosmic data. Its open rows were: amplitude ×1.8 low, gain slope ×1.5 shallow and curved, rise and FWHM too slow (needing either a ×2.4 faster ion or a ×5 weaker ion signal), and the neighbour-strip delay. The first three are addressed here; the neighbour delay is not.

The two mechanisms act on different observables, so they can be tested separately: feedback is prompt, so it changes the charge and not the shape; the ion species changes the shape and only indirectly the peak.

Every gain ladder is steeper than Garfield, and the excess is set by the gas

Local slope between neighbouring voltages, X view, clean points only; dashed: Garfield’s slope per gas

Ar/iso: data slope ×1.26–1.51 Garfield on three chambers bulked in April, May and June. It is the gas, not T14’s chamber.

Same chamber, gas changed: old det3 ×1.4 → ×3.1 in Ar/CF₄; det0 ×1.5 → ×3–7 in He/C₂H₆.

Every data ladder curves up; Garfield’s never does. No α(E) can give this curvature at real gain.

Threshold-free peak-strip max on M3-selected muons (same observable as T14). FRESH_LOOK §13.2, ladders_all.py.

3

Details

Data. June det3 (T14 chamber) Ar/iso 95/5; old det3 (bulked 5 May) Ar/iso then Ar/CF₄ 90/10 the next day; det0 (April; 6 mm drift gap) He/C₂H₆ 96.5/3.5 then Ar/iso. Threshold-free peak-strip maximum on M3-good rays, so the event population is the same at every voltage; fixed fiducial per chamber; quantile kept only if ≥ 5× the noise-only maximum and ≤ 0.7 × rail. Points excluded for time drift: det0 Ar/iso 490 V, old det3 Ar/iso 510 V, det0 He 505 V (out of sequence), Ar/CF₄ above 630 V (plateau).

Bias direction. All scans ran top-down in voltage and det0's gain rose with time (He: ×2–5 between the first and last 505 V points), which flattens measured slopes: det0's ratios are lower bounds.

Fits (fits_all.csv): exponential, G/(1−bG) with Garfield’s slope (2 parameters), and with a free slope. Runaway V* from the Garfield-slope fit: June det3 512–526 V, old det3 Ar/iso 516–533 V, Ar/CF₄ 638–638 V, He 510–527 V.

Why α(E) cannot do it. For any Townsend form the curvature is bounded by (s/V)(sV/ln G − 2); at real gains (ln G ≈ 10) that is 3–7× below what is measured. Penning, gas tables, water and the iso fraction are all α(E) changes.

Near runaway the amplitude distribution broadens, as a branching process must

Change of relative width of the peak-amplitude distribution vs distance from the fitted runaway voltage V*, X view

Pure gain scaling keeps the width fixed. A wrong α(E), a sagging gap or a field-map error multiply every avalanche alike.

Feedback broadens it near runaway. A random number of secondaries per avalanche (a branching process, mean βG → 1) spreads the amplitudes.

Seen in Ar/CF₄ and He/C₂H₆ in the last 10–20 V; flat in Ar/iso, which runs at βG ≈ 0.3–0.5. Also true inside 50 mm cells, so not spatial gain spread.

Noise-only floor subtracted where noted (det0 22 ADC, old det3 38 ADC). width_vs_v.py → width_vs_v.log.

4

Details

Space charge would narrow the distribution at high gain, the opposite sign. The higher quantiles also run away first (He: V* = 510 V on p90, 515 V on p75, 525 V on p50; June det3: βG higher on p50 than on p02), which is the same branching signature seen another way.

Caveat: near the noise floor the lowest quantile is lifted, which narrows the low-voltage widths and could fake broadening; hence the floor subtraction and the ≥ 3× floor cut. The Ar/CF₄ and He broadening survives both.

Literature: over-exponential Micromegas gain from photon feedback is known, and G/(1−βG) is the standard fit

sourcewhat it sayswhat it means here
Iguaz et al., microbulk Micromegas (arXiv:1110.2641, 1201.3012)“the gain curves for low quantities of isobutane show a deviation from the Rose and Korff gain model at high amplification fields. This over-exponential behaviour is due to the low quencher concentrations, which cannot avoid the production of secondary avalanches by the UV photons generated in the primary avalanche.” Ar/iC₄H₁₀ 1–35 %, 50 µm gap; also: resolution worsens below 5 % iso “as not all the UV photons … are absorbed”.Same gas family, same detector type: the effect we fit is reported, with the same attribution.
Şahin, Kowalski, Veenhof, JINST 11 P01003 (2016); NIM A 768 (2014); NIM A 718 (2013)“Production of the additional electron can be described with a single parameter β … G_T = G/(1 − βG)”, fitted together with Magboltz + Penning gains; β falls with quencher fraction and pressure, tied to the quencher’s photo-absorption cross section.Our gain model is exactly theirs: Garfield for G, plus one feedback parameter. β ≈ 2·10⁻⁵ here is in their range.
Peskov & Fonte, review (arXiv:0911.0463)“Detectors the cathode of which are not geometrically shielded from the avalanche emission, for example MICROMEGAS … can operate at high gains only in quenched gases”; feedback shows as “gain curve deviation from linear behaviour in log scale” because the feedback pulses are prompt (τ ≪ shaping time); photoemission rises steeply with photon energy.Explains why the pulse shape is untouched and why He (16–20 eV photons) feeds back more than Ar (~10 eV).
Garfield++ MPGD studies (arXiv:1606.04852; MPGD WG4 twiki; 2025 GEM pitch study arXiv:2505.03454)Simulated gains below measurement are common; Penning fixes much of it for THGEM; photon feedback is named as a missing process (Garfield does not emit electrons from electrodes).Our ×1.3–1.5 slope gap in Ar/iso is the same kind of known shortfall, with the curvature pointing at feedback rather than Penning.

5

Details

What the literature does not give us. (1) A measured β for Ar/iC₄H₁₀ 95/5 in a bulk Micromegas: Iguaz et al. show the over-exponential rise at “low quantities” of isobutane but the excerpt does not say where it stops; Şahin et al.’s β tables are for Ar–CO₂ and Ne–CO₂ in wire chambers. (2) A first-principles β: Garfield’s de-excitation model covers Ar levels, its optical data lacks isobutane, and it does not do photoemission from the mesh.

Not new, then, is the mechanism. What is new for us is its size at 5 % isobutane (βG ≈ 0.3–0.5 at G ≈ 2·10⁴), and the gas ordering Ar/iso < Ar/CF₄ ≈ He/C₂H₆ seen on the same chambers. My earlier prediction that He/C₂H₆ would feed back less was wrong; the photon-energy dependence of photoemission (Peskov & Fonte) is the likely reason.

Links: arXiv:1110.2641, arXiv:1201.3012, Şahin 2016 (Ne–CO₂), Şahin 2014 (Ar–CO₂), Peskov & Fonte, THGEM Garfield++, GEM pitch study, MPGD WG4.

6

Details

Why det0. Its 6 mm gap gives short columns (Ar/iso ~218 ns at ~27.5 µm/ns, He/C₂H₆ ~400 ns at ~15 µm/ns, Magboltz extrapolated to 1.33 kV/cm), and the same chamber and electronics ran He/C₂H₆, whose ions are ~5–10× faster than any ion in Ar. The toy models both gases (cluster statistics, drift, diffusion, gain spread, strips, sampling, selection, 50 %-edge alignment). The shaper time scale is fitted on He first (best rms 0.028 at tp 140 ns), then Ar’s (f, T) is scanned.

Result. At every shaper He allows, Ar⁺ with full signal (f 0.9, T 340 ns) is excluded (rms 0.17–0.19 vs a best of ~0.03). The best region is T ≈ 140–220 ns with f ≥ 0.5. Suppressed slow ions (f 0.2, T 340) are disfavoured (0.049–0.059) but not excluded, and at tp 150 a weak fast ion fits about as well: det0 rules out the chain’s ion, it does not by itself fix f.

A new tension. He calibrates the shaper at tp 130–150 ns, faster than the nominal 180 ns and the 166 ns from the noise autocorrelation. Either the shaper is faster, or the He column or He ion is mis-modelled. Open.

Earlier today I quoted a template fit (Ar = He pulse ⊗ ion) giving f 0.8–0.96, T 120–150 ns; that treated He as a point response, which the 6 mm gap and He’s slow drift make wrong. It is superseded by this toy.

Literature: the drifting ion is a hydrocarbon, and its mobility predicts the measured transit

T = g²/(K·V) at 490 V over the MX17 150 µm gap (pillar gerber), for the chain’s Ar⁺ and the measured hydrocarbon-ion mobilities

Cortez et al., JINST 14 P04010 (2019): in Ar–iC₄H₁₀, Ar⁺ charge-transfers to isobutane; the drifting ions are C₄Hₙ⁺ / C₈Hₙ⁺. K₀ at 95 % Ar: 2.08 (C₄), 1.74 (C₈) cm²/V·s (15 Td).

Giomataris (ICFA 1999): in Ar + 10 % iC₄H₁₀ “the electron signal and the ion tail are developed within 5 ns and 80 ns”, ion drift “typically within 100 ns” (100 µm gap).

Garfield Ar⁺ in Ar: K₀ 1.2 at our E/N (resonant charge exchange slows it). With the chain’s 150 µm gap this is its 352 ns.

K = K₀·N₀/N at 745.8 Torr, 293 K. Hydrocarbon K₀ are low-field (15 Td, 8 Torr); their high-field values are not measured.

7

Details

Ion identity. Cortez et al. assume the Ar⁺ → iC₄H₁₀ charge-transfer rate equals Ar⁺ → n-butane (1.4×10⁻⁹ cm³/s, Jiao et al. 2007), giving C₂–C₃ fragments that react on to C₄Hₙ⁺ and then C₈Hₙ⁺. At 1 atm with 5 % isobutane (n ≈ 1.2×10¹⁸ cm⁻³) the transfer takes ~1 ns, so essentially the whole transit is by hydrocarbon ions. At 8 Torr they see C₄Hₙ⁺ survive only above 80 % Ar; at 1 atm the C₄ → C₈ step is likely complete, so C₈Hₙ⁺ (K₀ 1.74) is the more probable carrier.

Gap. MX17's amplification gap is 150 µm, confirmed from the pillar gerber (T14 campaign), and the chain uses it. A 128 µm standard bulk would give ×0.73 shorter transits; that does not apply here.

Not settled. No measured high-field (~130–160 Td) mobility for these ions; non-resonant ions keep their mobility better than Ar⁺ at high E/N, but by how much is a guess. Giomataris’ 80–100 ns is a 100 µm gap at an unspecified voltage; scaled as g² to 150 µm (same field order) it is ~180–225 ns, consistent with the hydrocarbon prediction.

Links: Cortez 2019, Giomataris 1999, Coimbra LCTPC slides, ion mobility in Ar/Ne mixtures, Rao et al. (Ar⁺ at high E/N).

8

Details

Ion speed does not change the gain slope; feedback does not change the pulse shape. So the slope and curvature rows are feedback alone, the rise/FWHM rows are the ion alone, and only the amplitude row needs both.

The ion factor assumes f ≈ 0.9 (full ion signal). If the ion signal is weaker (det0 does not exclude f 0.5), the ion factor changes and feedback carries more of the amplitude.

What this does not rule out, and what is next

Not ruled out

• A weak but fast ion signal (f ≈ 0.5, or 0.2 at a 150 ns shaper) instead of a full fast one.

• A shaper faster than nominal: He says tp 130–150 ns, the noise ACF 166 ns, the cfg 180 ns.

• Feedback size from first principles: not computed; β is fitted, as in the literature.

• Hydrocarbon-ion mobility at 130–160 Td: not measured anywhere I found.

• Neighbour-strip delay and Y lobe: untouched by either effect.

Next (simulation only)

1. Chain: ion transit 140–220 ns (an exact time rescale) and rerun T14 shapes.

2. Chain: adopt G/(1−βG), β from the June ladder; re-quote amplitude.

3. Old det3 Ar/CF₄ shapes with the new Magboltz table: a second ion species (CF₃⁺).

4. Settle the shaper: He calibration vs noise ACF vs cfg.
